PUNITIVE DAMAGES AGAINST AN EMPLOYER IN A WRONGFUL-TERMINATION CASE (CIV. CODE §§ 3294, 3295; GOV. CODE § 818; WHITE V. ULTRAMAR; COLLEGE HOSPITAL; ADAMS V. MURAKAMI; ROBY V. MCKESSON) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PUNITIVE DAMAGES AGAINST AN EMPLOYER AFTER A TERMINATION — APPLICABILITY NOTE
This information sheet concerns Jordan Lee's former position as Assistant Store Manager with Acme, Inc., recorded here as having ended on August 28, 2026, a separation decision recorded here as having been made by or through a person holding the title Zone Manager, at an employer recorded here as being organized as California corporation. It describes what Civil Code sections 3294 and 3295, Government Code section 818, and four California Supreme Court decisions — Adams v. Murakami (1991), College Hospital Inc. v. Superior Court (1994), White v. Ultramar, Inc. (1999), and Roby v. McKesson Corp. (2009) — say about when punitive (exemplary) damages may be assessed against an employer on account of a termination: the statutory prerequisites of oppression, fraud, or malice proven by clear and convincing evidence; the statutory definitions of those terms; the separate limits section 3294, subdivision (b) places on employer liability for an employee's acts; who counts as a corporate employer's “officer, director, or managing agent”; what ratification means in this context; the requirement of evidence of the defendant's financial condition; the pretrial discovery, bifurcation, and pleading rules of section 3295; the federal constitutional limits on the size of an award; and the rule that a public entity is not liable for such damages. Whether any claim arising from Jordan Lee's separation exists at all, whether anyone acted with oppression, fraud, or malice, whether any person involved was an officer, director, or managing agent of Acme, Inc., and what amount (if any) a trier of fact could award are facts this sheet does not determine. Naming the parties, the date, the decisionmaker's title, and the employer's form here does not itself establish that any rule described below applies to this separation, and this sheet states what the statutes and the decisions say rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular claim or defense.

THE STATUTORY BASIS: CIVIL CODE SECTION 3294(A), A NONCONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION, AND PROOF BY CLEAR AND CONVINCING EVIDENCE
Civil Code section 3294, subdivision (a), is the general California statute authorizing exemplary (punitive) damages. By its own terms it applies “in an action for the breach of an obligation not arising from contract,” and it permits the plaintiff to recover damages “for the sake of example and by way of punishing the defendant” in addition to actual damages, but only “where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice.” Three features of that sentence are on the statute's face: the obligation breached must be one not arising from contract; the standard of proof is clear and convincing evidence rather than a preponderance; and the damages are additional to, not a substitute for, actual damages. In White v. Ultramar, Inc. (1999), the California Supreme Court reviewed a punitive damages award arising from a discharge — a jury had awarded the discharged employee $42,000 in compensatory damages and $300,000 in punitive damages on a claim that he was fired in retaliation for testifying at a former manager's unemployment hearing — and the Court recounted that before the statute's 1980 amendment courts had read section 3294 to make a California corporation liable for punitive damages only if the corporation itself, acting through those who managed its general affairs, engaged in the requisite oppression, fraud, or malice. Whether any obligation owed to Jordan Lee by Acme, Inc. was breached, whether any such obligation arose from contract or from some other source, and whether the clear-and-convincing standard could be met on these facts are matters this clause does not determine.

WHAT MUST BE PROVEN: THE STATUTORY DEFINITIONS OF MALICE, OPPRESSION, AND FRAUD, AND THE “DESPICABLE” REQUIREMENT
Civil Code section 3294, subdivision (c), supplies the definitions that control subdivision (a). “Malice” is defined as conduct intended by the defendant to cause injury to the plaintiff, or despicable conduct carried on by the defendant with a willful and conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others. “Oppression” is defined as despicable conduct that subjects a person to cruel and unjust hardship in conscious disregard of that person's rights. “Fraud” is defined as an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant, with the intention of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise causing injury. The word “despicable” and the clear-and-convincing standard entered the statute through the Willie L. Brown, Jr.-Bill Lockyer Civil Liability Reform Act of 1987; in College Hospital Inc. v. Superior Court (1994) the California Supreme Court described that Act as having increased the plaintiff's burden of proving punitive damages at trial to clear and convincing evidence, and stated that the statute's reference to “despicable” conduct seems to represent a new substantive limitation on punitive damage awards, using a powerful term that in its ordinary sense refers to circumstances that are base, vile, or contemptible. On that reading, where an intent to injure is absent, a willful and conscious disregard of the plaintiff's interests is not enough by itself: the additional component of despicable conduct must be found. Section 3294 also provides that the 1987 amendments apply to all actions in which the initial trial had not commenced before January 1, 1988. Whether anything done in connection with Jordan Lee's separation from Acme, Inc. meets any of these definitions is a fact this clause does not determine.

THE SEPARATE EMPLOYER LIMIT: CIVIL CODE SECTION 3294(B) AND THE FOUR ROUTES TO EMPLOYER LIABILITY
Even where an employee of a business has acted with oppression, fraud, or malice, Civil Code section 3294, subdivision (b), imposes a further and separate requirement before the employer itself can be assessed punitive damages for that employee's acts. The subdivision states that an employer shall not be liable for such damages based upon an employee's acts unless the employer (1) had advance knowledge of the unfitness of the employee and employed that person with a conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others, or (2) authorized the wrongful conduct, or (3) ratified it, or (4) was personally guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice. A second sentence adds a requirement specific to corporate employers: the advance knowledge and conscious disregard, the authorization, the ratification, or the act of oppression, fraud, or malice must be on the part of an officer, director, or managing agent of the corporation. In College Hospital the Court described the same tradition, stating that California has traditionally allowed punitive damages to be assessed against an employer for an employee's acts only where the circumstances indicate that the employer itself was guilty of fraud, oppression, or malice. In White the Court described the drafters' goals in adding subdivision (b) as avoiding punitive damages against employers who were merely negligent or reckless and distinguishing ordinary respondeat superior liability from corporate liability for punitive damages, and stated that for corporate punitive damages liability the wrongful act giving rise to exemplary damages must be committed by an officer, director, or managing agent. Whether any of these four routes describes Acme, Inc.'s relationship to the decision recorded as ending Jordan Lee's employment on August 28, 2026 is a fact this clause does not determine.

WHO IS A “MANAGING AGENT”: WHITE V. ULTRAMAR, INC. (1999)
White v. Ultramar, Inc. was decided to resolve a conflict among the Courts of Appeal over the meaning of “managing agent” in Civil Code section 3294, subdivision (b). The California Supreme Court held that a managing agent must be someone who exercises substantial discretionary authority over decisions that ultimately determine corporate policy, reasoning from the statute's placement of that term alongside “officer” and “director” that the Legislature intended to limit the class of employees whose exercise of discretion could result in a corporate employer's liability for punitive damages. The Court stated that supervisors with broad discretionary powers who exercise substantial discretionary authority in the corporation could be managing agents, while supervisors with no discretionary authority over decisions that ultimately determine corporate policy would not be, even though they may have the ability to hire or fire other employees; it explained that a contrary rule, treating any supervisor able to hire or fire as a managing agent, would allow punitive damages liability on no more than proof of simple tort liability. To demonstrate that an employee is a true managing agent, the Court said, a plaintiff seeking punitive damages would have to show that the employee exercised substantial discretionary authority over significant aspects of the corporation's business, and the scope of an employee's discretion and authority under that test is a question of fact decided case by case. Applying the test, the Court concluded that the zone manager who fired the plaintiff was a managing agent — her supervision of the plaintiff and her ability to fire him were alone insufficient, but she managed eight stores and at least sixty-five employees and so exercised substantial discretionary authority over vital aspects of the employer's business. Whether the person holding the title Zone Manager at Acme, Inc. exercised authority of that kind is a fact this clause does not determine.

WHAT “CORPORATE POLICY” MEANS IN THE TEST: ROBY V. MCKESSON CORP. (2009)
In Roby v. McKesson Corp. (2009) the California Supreme Court returned to the managing agent question in a case where a jury had awarded punitive damages against a large employer after the plaintiff's termination. The Court explained that a corporate defendant cannot be punished merely because one of its employees mistreated another employee in the workplace; the focus of the punitive damages inquiry is instead the corporation's own institutional responsibility, if any, for that conduct, a principle the Court said is codified in Civil Code section 3294, subdivision (b). Reading its earlier decision in White, the Court said that when it had spoken of persons having discretionary authority over corporate policy it was referring to formal policies that affect a substantial portion of the company and that are of the type likely to come to the attention of corporate leadership, and that it is this sort of broad authority that justifies punishing an entire company for an otherwise isolated act of oppression, fraud, or malice. Applying that understanding, the Court held that the record did not support the conclusion that the plaintiff's immediate supervisor — who supervised four employees at a local distribution center of a company with more than 20,000 employees — exercised that sort of broad authority or was a managing agent for purposes of section 3294, subdivision (b), so the reprehensibility of the employer's own conduct had to be assessed by looking to what its more senior managers knew and did. Whether Acme, Inc. had any institutional responsibility for the decision recorded as ending Jordan Lee's employment is a fact this clause does not determine.

RATIFICATION: WHAT AN EMPLOYER'S APPROVAL OF AN EMPLOYEE'S CONDUCT REQUIRES
Ratification is one of the routes to employer liability listed in Civil Code section 3294, subdivision (b). In College Hospital Inc. v. Superior Court (1994) the California Supreme Court described what the term means in this setting: for purposes of determining an employer's liability for punitive damages, ratification generally occurs where, under the particular circumstances, the employer demonstrates an intent to adopt or approve oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious behavior by an employee in the performance of the employee's job duties. The Court observed that the issue commonly arises where the employer or its managing agent is charged with failing to intercede in a known pattern of workplace abuse, or with failing to investigate or discipline the errant employee once the misconduct became known, and it stated that corporate ratification in the punitive damages context requires actual knowledge of the conduct and its outrageous nature. On the record before it, the Court concluded that the hospital administrator's conduct could not be characterized as ratification, because there was no evidence he knew of the harmful nature of the employee's conduct and because, by cautioning the employee, he had attempted to repudiate rather than adopt it. Whether anyone at Acme, Inc. knew of and adopted or approved any conduct connected with Jordan Lee's separation is a fact this clause does not determine.

EVIDENCE OF THE DEFENDANT'S FINANCIAL CONDITION: ADAMS V. MURAKAMI (1991)
Adams v. Murakami (1991) decided two questions about proof of a punitive damages award's size. The California Supreme Court held that an award of punitive damages cannot be sustained on appeal unless the trial record contains meaningful evidence of the defendant's financial condition, reasoning that a reviewing court cannot make a fully informed determination of whether an award is excessive without such evidence. The Court also held that the burden of introducing that evidence rests on the plaintiff rather than the defendant, resting that allocation on Evidence Code section 500, the traditional allocation of the burden of proof, and fundamental fairness. In explaining why the defendant's financial condition matters, the Court said that the purpose of punitive damages is not served by financially destroying a defendant — the purpose is to deter, not to destroy. Whether any evidence of Acme, Inc.'s financial condition exists or would be presented in any proceeding arising from Jordan Lee's separation is a fact this clause does not determine.

Superior Court (1994) the California Supreme Court described what the term means in this setting: for purposes of determining an employer's liability for punitive damages, ratification generally occurs where, under the particular circumstances, the employer demonstrates an intent to adopt or approve oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious behavior by an employee in the performance of the employee's job duties. The Court observed that the issue commonly arises where the employer or its managing agent is charged with failing to intercede in a known pattern of workplace abuse, or with failing to investigate or discipline the errant employee once the misconduct became known, and it stated that corporate ratification in the punitive damages context requires actual knowledge of the conduct and its outrageous nature. On the record before it, the Court concluded that the hospital administrator's conduct could not be characterized as ratification, because there was no evidence he knew of the harmful nature of the employee's conduct and because, by cautioning the employee, he had attempted to repudiate rather than adopt it. Whether anyone at Acme, Inc. knew of and adopted or approved any conduct connected with Jordan Lee's separation is a fact this clause does not determine.

expectedJSON.body: Adams v. Murakami (1991) decided two questions about proof of a punitive damages award's size. The California Supreme Court held that an award of punitive damages cannot be sustained on appeal unless the trial record contains meaningful evidence of the defendant's financial condition, reasoning that a reviewing court cannot make a fully informed determination of whether an award is excessive without such evidence. The Court also held that the burden of introducing that evidence rests on the plaintiff rather than the defendant, resting that allocation on Evidence Code section 500, the traditional allocation of the burden of proof, and fundamental fairness. In explaining why the defendant's financial condition matters, the Court said that the purpose of punitive damages is not served by financially destroying a defendant — the purpose is to deter, not to destroy. Whether any evidence of Acme, Inc.'s financial condition exists or would be presented in any proceeding arising from Jordan Lee's separation is a fact this clause does not determine.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code section 3295 governs how evidence of a defendant's profits and financial condition is handled before and during trial. Subdivision (e) provides that no claim for exemplary damages shall state an amount or amounts, so the sum sought is not pleaded in the complaint. Subdivision (a) allows a court, for good cause, to grant a defendant a protective order requiring the plaintiff to produce evidence of a prima facie case of liability for damages under section 3294 before evidence of the defendant's profits from the wrongful conduct or of the defendant's financial condition is introduced. Subdivision (c) prohibits pretrial discovery by the plaintiff as to that profits-and-financial-condition evidence unless the court enters an order permitting it; on the plaintiff's motion supported by appropriate affidavits, and after a hearing if the court deems one necessary, the court may enter such an order if it finds from the supporting and opposing affidavits that the plaintiff has established a substantial probability of prevailing on the section 3294 claim, and the statute adds that such an order is not a determination on the merits and may not be given in evidence or referred to at trial. Subdivision (d) requires the court, on any defendant's application, to exclude evidence of that defendant's profits or financial condition until after the trier of fact has returned a verdict for the plaintiff awarding actual damages and has found the defendant guilty of malice, oppression, or fraud, with that evidence then presented to the same trier of fact. Whether any of these procedures has been or would be invoked in a proceeding involving Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. is a fact this clause does not determine.

expectedJSON.body: A punitive damages award that satisfies Civil Code section 3294 is still subject to federal constitutional review for excessiveness. In Roby v. McKesson Corp. the California Supreme Court recited the three guideposts the United States Supreme Court articulated in State Farm Mut. Automobile Ins. Co. v. Campbell: the degree of reprehensibility of the defendant's misconduct; the disparity between the actual or potential harm suffered by the plaintiff and the punitive damages award; and the difference between the punitive damages awarded by the jury and the civil penalties authorized or imposed in comparable cases. Of these, the Court said, the most important is the degree of reprehensibility, which is assessed through five listed considerations: whether the harm caused was physical as opposed to economic; whether the conduct evinced an indifference to or a reckless disregard of the health or safety of others; whether the target of the conduct had financial vulnerability; whether the conduct involved repeated actions or was an isolated incident; and whether the harm resulted from intentional malice, trickery, or deceit rather than mere accident. Applying that test to the employment record before it, the Court concluded that a one-to-one ratio between compensatory and punitive damages was the federal constitutional limit in that case, basing the conclusion on the case's specific facts and noting in particular the relatively low degree of reprehensibility on the employer's part and the substantial compensatory verdict, which included a substantial award of noneconomic damages. The Court also stated that a defendant's wealth is relevant to whether an award has the appropriate deterrent effect but that the award must not punish a defendant simply for being wealthy. What ratio or amount, if any, would be constitutionally permissible in a proceeding arising from Jordan Lee's separation is a matter this clause does not determine.

Of the three guideposts that the high court outlined in State Farm, supra, 538 U.S. at page 418, the most important is the degree of reprehensibility of the defendant’s conduct.

the harm caused was physical as opposed to economic; [2] the tortious conduct evinced an indifference to or a reckless disregard of the health or safety of others; [3] the target of the conduct had financial vulnerability; [4] the conduct involved repeated actions or was an isolated incident; and [5] the harm was the result of intentional malice, trickery, or deceit, or mere accident.

After applying the test that the high court articulated in State Farm, supra, 538 U.S. at page 418, we conclude that a one-to-one ratio between compensatory and punitive damages is the federal constitutional limit here. We base this conclusion on the specific facts of this case.

We note in particular the relatively low degree of reprehensibility on the part of employer McKesson and the substantial compensatory damages verdict, which included a substantial award of noneconomic damages.

It is certainly relevant for a reviewing court to consider the wealth of a defendant when applying federal constitutional limits to an award of punitive damages, thereby ensuring that the award has the appropriate deterrent effect, but the punitive damages award must not punish the defendant simply for being wealthy.

expectedJSON.body: Government Code section 818 addresses punitive damages against public entities. It provides, notwithstanding any other provision of law, that a public entity is not liable for damages awarded under Section 3294 of the Civil Code or other damages imposed primarily for the sake of example and by way of punishing the defendant. The section is part of the statutory scheme on the liability of public entities and public employees, and by its terms it removes the category of punitive or exemplary damages from what may be awarded against a public entity, whatever the underlying claim. Whether Acme, Inc., recorded here as organized as California corporation, is a public entity within the meaning of that scheme is a question this clause does not answer.
